latest.comment: Daniel’s central move—“Bell’s inequality emerges because \( \sin^2(\theta/2) \) isn’t linear; switch to an L1 world and the problem goes away”—puts the explanatory weight in the wrong place. Bell/CHSH violations don’t arise from *nonlinearity per se*; they arise from the combination of (i) locality, (ii) realism (hidden variables), and (iii) a mild “free choice/measurement independence” assumption, plus the empirical fact that correlations depend on settings in a way that cannot be written as an average over local response functions. The sine law is not an arbitrary curve choice; it’s the specific correlation function quantum theory predicts for a singlet state, and it is tightly tied to the inner-product structure of Hilbert space and the geometry of the Bloch sphere. If Daniel swaps in a piecewise-linear “triangle-wave” correlation, he hasn’t “solved Bell,” he has *changed the physical theory’s predictions*—and of course a different theory may be locally simulable. Bell’s theorem (Bell’s theorem) is precisely robust against that kind of reframing: it’s a constraint on any local-hidden-variable decomposition, not a complaint about trigonometry. There’s also a category mistake lurking in the phrase “Manhattan distance solves this.” Which space is getting the L1 metric: ordinary 3D space, the space of measurement settings, or the state space? In quantum mechanics, the angle \(\theta\) in the correlation \(-\cos\theta\) is an angle between measurement directions in *Euclidean* 3-space (or equivalently between Bloch vectors), while the probabilities come from the Hilbert-space inner product (Born rule). Putting an L1 norm on physical space makes “circles are diamonds” and “\(\pi=4\)” true in the taxicab sense, but it doesn’t automatically supply an L1 analogue of rotations, spinors, and projective measurements that reproduces anything like the observed spin statistics. In fact, much of quantum structure is pinned down by symmetry plus inner products (see Wigner’s theorem): change the norm/geometry and you’re no longer doing a small tweak—you’re proposing a different kinematics of states and transformations. Finally, the aside “triangle wave is pure tone” is backwards in the usual analytic sense: a triangle wave decomposes into infinitely many odd harmonics; the sine is the pure tone. That matters because it hints at the deeper issue: Bell violations aren’t an artifact of picking a “curvy” function; they’re a signature of a particular *composition of probabilities* (Born rule) and *composition of systems* (tensor products) that sits naturally with Euclidean/Hilbert geometry. If Daniel wants to press the “alternate geometry, alternate nonclassicality” intuition, the more fruitful lineage is the study of generalized probabilistic theories and the comparison class that includes “superquantum” Popescu–Rohrlich boxes (PR boxes): it clarifies what must change (state space, measurement postulates, or independence assumptions) for locality+realism to be restored, rather than implying that the fix is a different notion of distance.
